body.statement: The minimax values obey \(V_n=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\{\inf_{\pi_n\in\Pi_n}\sum_{m=1}^M\lambda_mL_n(\pi_n,m)-\sum_{m=1}^M\lambda_mc_{n,m}\}\) and \(V=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\{\inf_{u\in\mathcal U}\sum_{m=1}^M\lambda_mL(u,m)-\sum_{m=1}^M\lambda_mc_m\}\), with attained least-favorable priors. For every \(\epsilon>0\), a finite mixture of Bayes best responses that are Markov in \((t,(X_j(t),Q_j(t))_{j\in\mathcal J},(b_m^\lambda)_{m=1}^M)\) is an \(\epsilon\)-saddle control and has every scenario regret at most \(V+\epsilon\).
body.justification: The least-favorable prior converts robust enrichment into posterior-state control without mistaking one Bayes rule for a minimax policy.
body.gap: Burnett and Jennison and Ballarini et al. take the prior as an input; they do not construct the adversarial prior or a simultaneous scenario-risk saddle mixture.
body.consumer: It supplies the robust scenario weights and policy mixture needed to populate a confirmatory trial design specification.
body.proof_tex:
We give one argument that applies to the finite and diffusion experiments.
Write \(\mathcal A\) for the relevant policy class and
\[
r(a)=(L(a,1)-c_1,\ldots,L(a,M)-c_M)\in[0,1]^M,
\]
using \(n\)-subscripts in the finite experiment.  Let
\[
C:=\overline{\{r(a):a\in\mathcal A\}}\subset[0,1]^M.
\]
Time-zero randomization, which is allowed by both Definitions
\(\mathrm{def:finite\text{-}policy\text{-}class}\) and
\(\mathrm{def:continuous\text{-}control\text{-}class}\), makes \(C\) convex;
it is compact by construction.

Put \(v=\min_{r\in C}\max_mr_m\).  The set
\(D=C+\mathbb R_+^M\) is closed and convex, and \(v\mathbf1\) is a boundary
point of \(D\).  Indeed, compactness attains the minimum, so some
\(r^\star\in C\) satisfies \(r^\star\leq v\mathbf1\), whereas
\((v-a)\mathbf1\notin D\) for every \(a>0\).  Project
\((v-k^{-1})\mathbf1\) onto \(D\).  The projection inequality, followed by
normalization and passage to a subsequence, supplies a nonzero supporting
normal \(\lambda^\star\).  Because \(D\) is upward closed, every coordinate
of this normal is nonnegative; normalize it so that
\(\sum_m\lambda_m^\star=1\).  The support inequality is
\[
\lambda^{\star\top}r\geq
\lambda^{\star\top}(v\mathbf1)=v
\quad\text{for every }r\in C.
\tag{18}
\]
Conversely, for every \(\lambda\in\Delta_M\),
\(\lambda^\top r\leq\max_mr_m\), whence
\[
\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\min_{r\in C}\lambda^\top r=v.
\tag{19}
\]
No continuity of the terminal loss was used in this finite-dimensional
separation.

Closure does not alter an infimum of a linear functional.  In the finite
experiment,
\[
\inf_{r\in C}\lambda^\top r
=\inf_{\pi_n\in\Pi_n}\sum_m\lambda_m
\{L_n(\pi_n,m)-c_{n,m}\}
=B_n(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_{n,m}.
\]
The same calculation with \(u\in\mathcal U\) gives
\(B(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_m\).  Substitution in (19) proves both
displayed minimax identities.  The dual objective is \(1\)-Lipschitz:
\[
\left|\inf_{r\in C}\lambda^\top r-
\inf_{r\in C}\lambda'^\top r\right|
\leq\sup_{r\in[0,1]^M}|(\lambda-\lambda')^\top r|
\leq\|\lambda-\lambda'\|_1.
\]
It is therefore continuous on compact \(\Delta_M\), so a least-favorable
prior is attained in both experiments.

We next identify the sufficient posterior state and the saddle response.
Fix a prior \(\lambda\).  Under the zero-drift reference law and any
scenario-independent observed control, conditional Gaussian integration
gives the likelihood ratio
\[
Z_m(X(t),Q(t))
=\exp\!\left\{\sum_jh_j^mX_j(t)
-\frac12\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_j(t)\right\}.
\tag{20}
\]
The denominator \(\sum_r\lambda_rZ_r\) is strictly positive because every
\(Z_r>0\) and at least one \(\lambda_r>0\).  Bayes' formula and (20) give
\[
\Pr\{m\mid\mathcal F_t\}
=\frac{\lambda_mZ_m(X(t),Q(t))}
{\sum_r\lambda_rZ_r(X(t),Q(t))}
=b_m^\lambda(X(t),Q(t)).
\tag{21}
\]
Moreover,
\[
\sum_m\lambda_mL(u,m)
=\mathbb E_0^u\!\left[
\sum_m\lambda_mZ_m(X(1),Q(1))\ell_m(X(1),Q(1))
\right].
\tag{22}
\]
Thus the Bayes control problem is a terminal-cost Markov problem in
\((t,X,Q,b^\lambda)\), with \(b^\lambda\) itself the deterministic function
in (21).

For clarity, Markovization can be obtained directly in this Gaussian model.
For a relaxed observed control, disintegrate its action at time \(t\)
conditionally on \((X(t),Q(t),b^\lambda(t))\), and use that conditional
simplex vector as the randomized Markov action.  For simple controls,
iterated conditional Gaussian kernels show by induction that this operation
preserves the terminal reference-law distribution.  Approximation by simple
predictable controls, using the bounded-energy estimate (10) from the proof
of \(\mathrm{thm:boundary\text{-}stable\text{-}frontier}\), extends the
identity to all admissible relaxed controls.  Equations (20)--(22) then show
that it preserves every scenario risk, not only their Bayes average.
Consequently every Bayes response may be chosen Markov in the state displayed
in the theorem.

Finally choose the attained least-favorable prior \(\lambda^\star\).
The compact weak relaxed-control formulation attains the nonnegative,
lower-semicontinuous Bayes terminal cost: each
\(\mathbf1\{a_j<0\}\) is lower semicontinuous because \(a_j\) is continuous,
and (22) has the positive continuous likelihood weights.  Equivalently, one
may take a minimizing sequence, extract a weak relaxed-control limit, and
apply the defining open-set inequality term by term.  Let \(F\) be the set
of risk vectors of its Bayes best responses.  From (18), every member of
\(F\) has \(\lambda^{\star\top}r=V\).  A minimax vector
\(r^\star\in C\) satisfies \(r^\star\leq V\mathbf1\), and
\[
V\leq\lambda^{\star\top}r^\star\leq V,
\]
so \(r^\star\) lies in the exposed Bayes face.  Approximating within that
face by attained Markov Bayes responses and applying the finite-dimensional
Carathéodory reduction yields a mixture of at most \(M+1\) such responses
whose risk vector is at most \((V+\epsilon)\mathbf1\).  The mixture seed is
drawn at time zero and included in the exogenous randomization, so the
mixture remains admissible and each component is Markov in
\((t,X,Q,b^{\lambda^\star})\).

For this mixture \(u^\epsilon\), for every nature prior \(\lambda\),
\[
\sum_m\lambda_mr_m(u^\epsilon)\leq V+\epsilon,
\]
while for every control \(u\), (18) gives
\[
\sum_m\lambda_m^\star r_m(u)\geq V.
\]
These are the two saddle inequalities, and taking point-mass \(\lambda\)
in the first one gives \(r_m(u^\epsilon)\leq V+\epsilon\) for every
scenario.  Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:null\text{-}boundary\text{-}closure}\)
keeps all of these best responses and priors on the declared finite scenario
game; it is not used to add an unlisted alternative.
